name: Graphic Design with Canva
objectives: Given a design request from a client, employer or your own project, write a design brief that names the audience, the main message, the format and the size, with all four parts in one short paragraph
Given a draft design, arrange text and images using hierarchy, alignment, contrast, repetition and white space, so a viewer can tell the main message within 3 seconds

Using Canva's free plan, build a design at the right size from a template or a blank page, changing the text, colors, fonts and images, using no more than 2 fonts and 3 main colors and no paid elements
Before you share or print a design, check the design for readable contrast, correct spelling and facts, and the right to use every image, fixing every problem you find
When a design is finished, export the design in the right file type and add it to a portfolio with a short description, PDF for print and PNG or JPG for screens, with a clear file name

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What graphic designers do, and the design brief
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a design brief that names the audience, message, format and size.
This lesson builds toward: Given a design request from a client, employer or your own project, you will write a design brief that names the audience, the main message, the format and the size, with all four parts in one short paragraph.
Graphic designers use pictures, words, colors and layout to get a message across. They make flyers, social media posts, menus, signs, logos, slides and reports. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics says employers look closely at a portfolio: a collection of your best work.
Design work comes in many forms: an in-house job at a company or nonprofit, a social media or marketing assistant role, a print shop, or freelance work for local businesses. Many design jobs ask for a degree or technical training, but a strong portfolio helps at every level. Software certifications, such as Adobe Certified Professional (exams delivered by Certiport), can give an edge later. This course prepares you to make a first portfolio piece; it does not grant a certificate.
Every good design starts with a brief: a short plan that answers four questions. Who is it for (the audience)? What is the one main message? What format is it (flyer, social post, poster, menu)? What size is it? If you cannot answer these, ask the client before you start.
Step by step:
- Ask who the design is for.
- Ask for the one main message and any must-have details (date, place, price, contact).
- Ask what format it is and where it will be used.
- Write down the size, such as letter size for a flyer or square for a social post.
- Read the brief back to the client and get a yes before you design.
Words to know:
- Graphic design: using words, pictures, colors and layout to share a message.
- Design brief: a short written plan for a design: audience, message, format and size.
- Portfolio: a collection of your best work that you show employers or clients.
- Freelance: working for yourself and doing paid projects for different clients.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Graphic Designers
- Certiport: Adobe Certified Professional
Try it now: Pick a real or practice client, such as a car wash fundraiser, a barbershop or your own side business. Write a brief in one paragraph that names the audience, the main message, the format and the size. Keep it for the final task.
You can now say what graphic designers make and write a four-part design brief.

check.q: Which of these belongs in a design brief?
options: The audience, main message, format and size
A list of every font you know
check.why: A brief answers who it is for, what it says, what it is and how big it is.

check.q: A client says, "Make me a flyer." What do you do first?
options: Copy a flyer from another business
Ask about the audience, message and size, and write a brief
check.why: Asking first and writing a brief stops wasted work and redesigns.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Layout rules that make a design easy to read
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Arrange a design so the main message stands out first.
This lesson builds toward: Given a draft design, you will arrange text and images using hierarchy, alignment, contrast, repetition and white space, so a viewer can tell the main message within 3 seconds.
People look at a flyer or post for only a few seconds. Five simple rules help them get the message fast.
Hierarchy: make the most important thing the biggest or boldest, then the next most important, then the details. Alignment: line things up along the same edge or center line so the design looks tidy. Contrast: make important things look different, for example dark text on a light background or a big headline next to small details.
Repetition: use the same colors, fonts and shapes again so the design feels like one piece. White space: leave empty space around things. Empty space is not wasted; it lets the eye rest and makes the main message stand out.
A quick test: show your design to someone for 3 seconds, then hide it. Ask what it was about. If they cannot say the main message, make the headline bigger and cut extra words.
Step by step:
- Choose the one main message and make it the biggest text.
- Put the details (date, place, contact) in smaller text.
- Line up text and images along the same edges.
- Use the same colors and fonts again.
- Remove anything that does not help the message.
- Do the 3-second test with another person.
Words to know:
- Hierarchy: showing what is most important first by making it bigger, bolder or higher on the page.
- Alignment: lining things up along the same edge or center line.
- Contrast: a clear difference, such as dark on light or big next to small.
- White space: empty space around and between things in a design.
Try it now: Find a flyer or ad around you (on a wall, in the mail or online). On paper, list the five rules and mark which ones it uses well and which it breaks. Then sketch a better layout for your own brief: headline, picture and details in boxes.
You can now use hierarchy, alignment, contrast, repetition and white space to plan a layout, and test it in 3 seconds.

check.q: On an event flyer, what should usually be the biggest text?
options: The main message, such as the event name
check.why: Hierarchy puts the main message first so people get it in seconds.

check.q: Your design feels crowded. Which fix follows the layout rules?
options: Cut extra words and leave more white space
Make all the text the same size
check.why: White space and fewer words let the main message stand out.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choosing colors and fonts
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a simple color palette and font pair that are easy to read.
This lesson builds toward: Given a draft design, you will arrange text and images using hierarchy, alignment, contrast, repetition and white space, so a viewer can tell the main message within 3 seconds. Before you share or print a design, you will check the design for readable contrast, correct spelling and facts, and the right to use every image, fixing every problem you find.
Keep it simple: pick 2 or 3 main colors plus a neutral such as white, black or gray. If the client has brand colors, use those. Using the same colors on every piece makes a business easy to recognize.
Use no more than 2 fonts: one for headlines and one for body text. A bold, simple font works for headlines. A plain, easy-to-read font works for details. Fancy script fonts are hard to read at small sizes, so save them for a word or two.
Text must stand out from its background. The web accessibility guidelines (WCAG, from the W3C) ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. A free contrast checker, such as WebAIM's, tells you the ratio when you type in the two colors. Light gray text on white, or red on green, often fails.
Step by step:
- Write down 2 or 3 main colors and one neutral.
- Pick one headline font and one body font.
- Check each text color against its background in a contrast checker.
- Change any pair that is below 4.5 to 1 for normal text.
Words to know:
- Color palette: the small set of colors you use in a design.
- Font: a style of letters, such as bold block letters or handwriting style.
- Contrast ratio: a number that shows how different two colors are in brightness; higher is easier to read.
- Brand colors: the set colors a business or group always uses so people recognize it.
Official sources:
- W3C: Understanding Contrast (Minimum)
- WebAIM Contrast Checker
Try it now: For your brief, write down 2 or 3 colors and one neutral, and choose a headline font and a body font. Open a free contrast checker, type in your text color and background color, and write down the ratio. Change any pair under 4.5 to 1.
You can now choose a simple color palette and font pair and check that the text is readable.

check.q: How many fonts should a simple flyer usually use?
options: A different font for every line
check.why: One headline font and one body font keep a design clean and readable.

check.q: A contrast checker shows your normal-size text is 2.8 to 1. What do you do?
options: Make the text darker or the background lighter until it is at least 4.5 to 1
Leave it; any ratio is fine
Add a second background color behind it
check.why: WCAG asks for at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text so most people can read it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a design in Canva's free plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a design at the right size from a template and make it your own.
This lesson builds toward: Using Canva's free plan, you will build a design at the right size from a template or a blank page, changing the text, colors, fonts and images, using no more than 2 fonts and 3 main colors and no paid elements.
Canva works in a web browser at canva.com or in the Canva app. Make a free account with your email. The free plan includes many templates, fonts, photos and graphics. Some items are only for paid plans and are marked as Pro or premium; leave those out so your design stays free.
Start with the size. Use the search or the create button and type the format you need, such as "Flyer" or "Instagram post". Canva opens a page at that size. You can also set a custom size. Schools, students and nonprofits may qualify for free upgraded plans; check Canva's own Education and Nonprofits pages.
A template is a ready-made design. It is a starting point, not the finished work. Change the words to your brief, change the colors to your palette, use your two fonts, swap in your own photos, and delete anything that does not help the message. Employers can spot a template that was not changed.
Use the side panel to add text, shapes and graphics, and to upload your own photos. Canva saves your work as you go. Give your design a clear name so you can find it again.
Step by step:
- Sign in to Canva on a computer or the app.
- Search for the format you need, such as Flyer, or set a custom size.
- Pick a template that fits your layout sketch, or start blank.
- Replace the text with your brief's message and details.
- Change the colors and fonts to your palette and font pair.
- Upload your own photos or use free images you are allowed to use.
- Delete anything that does not help the message, then name the design.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you change to make your own.
- Free plan: the version of Canva you can use without paying.
- Pro or premium item: a template, photo or graphic that needs a paid plan.
- Custom size: a page size you type in yourself, in inches, pixels or millimeters.
Official sources:
- Canva
- Canva for Education (check who qualifies)
- Canva for Nonprofits (check who qualifies)
Try it now: Open Canva, search for Flyer and pick a template that matches your sketch from Lesson 2. Change the text, colors and fonts to your brief and palette, add one photo you took yourself, and delete anything extra. Name the design with the client and date.
You can now build a design in Canva's free plan at the right size and change a template so it fits your brief.

check.q: You need a flyer in Canva. What do you do first?
options: Search for the Flyer format or set the right size
check.why: Starting at the right size saves you from redoing the layout later.

check.q: You want your design to stay free. A graphic is marked as Pro. What do you do?
options: Use it and hope no one notices
check.why: Pro items need a paid plan; choosing free items keeps the design free and properly licensed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Images, rights and the final check
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a design for rights, readability, spelling and facts before you share it.
This lesson builds toward: Before you share or print a design, you will check the design for readable contrast, correct spelling and facts, and the right to use every image, fixing every problem you find.
Not every picture online is free to use. In the US, a work is protected by copyright as soon as it is created, even without a © mark. That means you cannot copy a photo, logo or drawing from a website or another business just because you found it.
Safe images are ones you took or made yourself, images inside Canva that your plan lets you use (read Canva's license terms on its site), and images from free sources whose license clearly allows your use. Never use another company's logo, a celebrity's photo or a sports team's mark without written permission. If you use AI to make an image, check the tool's rules and check the image for mistakes such as strange hands or wrong text.
Before you share or print, do the final check: Is the main message clear in 3 seconds? Is every text color readable (contrast)? Is every word spelled right, and are the date, time, place, price and contact correct? Do you have the right to use every image and font? Ask the client or another person to read it too. When you post online, add alt text (a short description of the image) if the site allows it, so people who use screen readers know what it shows.
Step by step:
- Do the 3-second test again.
- Check every text color against its background.
- Read every word slowly, out loud, for spelling.
- Check the date, time, place, price and contact against the brief.
- List where each image came from and why you may use it.
- Ask someone else to read it, then fix what they find.
Words to know:
- Copyright: the legal right of the person who made a work to control copies of it.
- License: permission, with rules, to use someone else's work.
- Alt text: a short written description of an image for people who cannot see it.
- Proofread: read slowly to find and fix mistakes.
Official sources:
- US Copyright Office: Copyright basics FAQ
- W3C: Understanding Contrast (Minimum)
Try it now: Run the final check on your Canva flyer. Write a list of every image and where it came from. Read every word out loud, compare the details with your brief, and check one text color in a contrast checker. Fix every problem you find.
You can now check a design for rights, readability, spelling and facts, and fix it before you share it.

check.q: You find a great photo on another bakery's website with no © mark. Can you use it on your client's flyer?
options: No; it is still protected, so use your own or a licensed image
Yes, because it has no © mark
Yes, if you make it smaller
Yes, if you change its color
check.why: Copyright protects a work once it is made, mark or not.

check.q: Which step is part of the final check before printing?
options: Comparing the date, place and price with the brief
check.why: Wrong details on a printed flyer cost the client money and trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Exporting, getting feedback and building a portfolio
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Export a design in the right file type and add it to a portfolio with a description.
This lesson builds toward: When a design is finished, you will export the design in the right file type and add it to a portfolio with a short description, PDF for print and PNG or JPG for screens, with a clear file name. Using Canva's free plan, you will build a design at the right size from a template or a blank page, changing the text, colors, fonts and images, using no more than 2 fonts and 3 main colors and no paid elements.
When the design passes the final check, share it for feedback before the final export. Canva has a Share button where you can send a view link. Ask one clear question, such as "Is anything unclear or wrong?", then make the changes the client agrees on.
Export in the right file type. Open Share and choose Download. Use PDF for anything that will be printed, such as a flyer. Use PNG for social media posts and graphics with text, because it keeps text sharp. JPG is fine for photos where a smaller file matters. Name the file clearly, for example: carwash-flyer-2026-11.pdf.
Make a matching piece. Start a new design at the social post size and use the same colors, fonts and photo, so the set looks like one campaign. Clients often want a flyer and a post together.
Add the work to your portfolio. A portfolio can be a folder, a free website or a simple PDF. For each piece, write 3 to 4 sentences: the goal, who it was for, the design choices you made and the result. Only show client work if the client says yes, and never include private details.
Step by step:
- Share a view link and ask one clear feedback question.
- Make the agreed changes.
- Open Share, then Download, and pick PDF for print or PNG for screens.
- Name the file with the project and date.
- Make a matching social post with the same colors and fonts.
- Write a 3 to 4 sentence portfolio description and add both files.
Words to know:
- Export: to save a design as a file you can print, post or send.
- PDF: a file type that keeps the layout the same everywhere; best for printing.
- PNG: an image file type that keeps text and edges sharp; good for screens.
- JPG: an image file type that makes photos smaller; text can look a little blurry.
Try it now: Share your flyer with one person and ask, "Is anything unclear or wrong?" Fix what they find. Download the flyer as a PDF, make a matching square post and download it as a PNG, name both files clearly, and write your 3 to 4 sentence portfolio description.
You can now get feedback, export a design in the right file type, make a matching piece and add it to a portfolio with a description.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Design brief The brief is missing the audience, the message, the format or the size. One short paragraph names all four parts. It also lists the must-have details and was read back to the client. Layout A viewer cannot say the main message after 3 seconds, or the layout looks crowded. The main message is clearly first, things line up and there is white space. The flyer and post use the same layout ideas so they read as one set. Built in Canva Wrong size, more than 2 fonts, a paid item, or an unchanged template. Right size, no more than 2 fonts and 3 main colors, free items only, and the template is made their own. Started from a blank page or changed the template so much it is clearly their own design. Checked A spelling or detail mistake, unreadable text, or an image with no clear right to use it. No mistakes, text passes 4.5 to 1, and every image is listed with where it came from. Another person proofread it and alt text is written for the post. Exported and described Wrong file type, unclear file name, or no description. Flyer as PDF, post as PNG, clear file names, and a 3 to 4 sentence description. The description explains why each design choice fits the audience, and the client agreed to it being shown. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Your flyer is going to a print shop. Which file type is best?
options: A PNG made for a phone
check.why: PDF keeps the layout the same and is the usual choice for printing.

check.q: What belongs in a portfolio description?
options: The goal, who it was for, your design choices and the result
check.why: A short story of the goal, choices and result shows employers how you think.
